Understanding memory allocation in Rust

Published by Alice Chen on 2025-02-01

Memory allocation is one of the most important concepts to understand when writing systems software in Rust. Unlike garbage collected languages, Rust gives you direct control over when and where memory is allocated. This post explains the difference between stack and heap allocation and how the ownership system enforces safety.

Stack allocation

Local variables in Rust are allocated on the stack by default. The stack is fast because allocation is just a pointer bump. When a function returns, all its stack frames are freed instantly. This makes stack allocation essentially free in terms of performance overhead. The compiler knows the exact size at compile time.

Heap allocation

When you need dynamic sizing or values that outlive their scope, you use the heap via Box, Vec, or String. Heap allocation involves asking the allocator for memory, which is slower than stack allocation. The ownership system ensures that heap memory is freed exactly once when the owning variable goes out of scope.

Measuring allocations

You can use tools like valgrind and the built-in allocator API to count allocations in your programs. Reducing unnecessary heap allocations is a common optimization technique in performance-sensitive Rust code. Profile before optimizing to find the actual bottlenecks in your allocation patterns and memory usage overhead costs.

References: The Rustonomicon, Rust Reference Manual section 6.2
